newsitem.title: JAPAN: Former Nomura chief arrested, scandal could widen.
newsitem.headline: Former Nomura chief arrested, scandal could widen.

text.p: A former president of Nomura Securities was arrested on Friday over a racketeer scandal and fresh revelations looked likely to further entangle a top Japanese bank in the ever-widening affair.

Cabinet ministers from the prime minister down greeted the new evidence of corporate misdeeds with expressions of outrage, and speculation mounted that more institutions will be ensnared before the end of the saga, which has further tarnished the image of Japan's financial sector.

Prosecutors said Hideo Sakamaki, who stepped down as Nomura president in March over the scandal, was arrested on suspicion of conspiring with three Nomura executives to pay 38.5 million yen ($331,000) in 1995 to Ryuichi Koike, a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer at the heart of the affair.

"Sokaiya" buy stakes in firms and extort money from them by threatening to disrupt shareholders' meetings with embarrassing questions. Paying off sokaiya was made illegal in 1982, but the practice has proven tough to stamp out.
Three Nomura executives, as well as Ryuichi Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori, have already been arrested, but the brokerage had denied that other top management was involved.

Junichi Ujiie, who took over as Nomura president on May 1 as part of a sweeping management shake-up, conceded at a news conference on Friday that Sakamaki's arrest raised suspicions that the company itself was involved in the scandal.
The scandal is the second to hit Nomura, Japan's biggest brokerage, in six years -- which many think will mean a stiff punishment this time around.

In another twist, the Finance Ministry said Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) had lent 3.16 billion yen ($27.2 million) in 1989 to a firm run by the younger Koike to buy shares in Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, including Nomura.

Top DKB executives said last week they would step down to take responsibility for dubious loans to the younger Koike and his firm. They also admitted the bank may have hidden improper transactions from Finance Ministry inspectors.
The bank faces administrative penalties for the violation and some executives could be hit with breach of trust charges.
Nomura faces as yet undetermined administrative penalties and has already lost many clients since the scandal broke.

It will have to fight fiercely to restore its credibility, although analysts noted it managed to be the most profitable of Japanese brokerages last month and remains a likely winner as Japan implements its "Big Bang" financial reforms.

Perhaps more critically, the scandal is testing officials' resolve to punish misdeeds and tighten surveillance as they start to cut the web of regulations that have kept Tokyo's financial sector in a protective cocoon for decades.
Political leaders vowed again on Friday to clean up the financial sector to restore credibility at home and abroad.
"The government wants a no-holds-barred, fully fledged investigation into the scandal to restore public confidence in the entire securities industry," said Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, forced to resign his finance portfolio in 1991 over brokerage and banking scandals, told reporters the affair would deal a heavy blow to the securities industry. "The impact this will have is more severe than you think," he said.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said he would urge Japan's securities watchdog to push on with investigations of Nomura and warned of tough action once the probe is completed.
"The fact that the government and the prosecutors are acting sternly will gain understanding overseas," he said.

Finance Ministry officials, their own images tarnished by a series of policy missteps in recent years, are also in the hot seat. Critics charge that the ministry should have uncovered the dubious loans by DKB, though officials say this is all but impossible if banks try to hide such deals.

On Thursday, parliament's Lower House passed a bill to set up a new government agency, separate from the Finance Ministry, to police the financial sector. But experts worry the new watchdog, to be set up next year, will lack sufficient funds and staff to tackle the tough task ahead. ($1=116)
